strengths: The paper presents a timely and systematic investigation into adapting Mamba (state-space models) to speech self-supervised learning (HuBERT), addressing a clear gap where previous works focused only on isolated downstream tasks.

Comprehensive experimental evaluation that covers computational efficiency (MACs, RTF vs. sequence length up to 320s), long-context document-level ASR, streaming/causal ASR, and SUPERB probing benchmarks.

Insightful layer-wise representation analyses using both k-means phone purity and Canonical Correlation Analysis (CCA) across phone, speaker, and emotion representations, providing good interpretability.

Fair and transparent reporting of results, highlighting not only where Mamba shines (e.g., causal streaming ASR, memory efficiency in long-context modeling) but also where it struggles (scalability in bidirectional settings at the base model size).
weaknesses: Due to hardware constraints, the models were pretrained on a single GPU with one-fourth the audio duration per batch compared to standard HuBERT, which may limit the absolute convergence and representation quality compared to standard public checkpoints.

The document-level ASR comparison compares Mamba only against a vanilla full-attention Transformer (which trivially encounters OOM), omitting standard long-context or efficient attention baselines such as chunked/local attention, Conformer with relative positional encodings, or linear attention variants.

Downstream probing is evaluated on only four selected tasks from SUPERB (PR, SID, ER, IC) rather than the complete benchmark suite, which leaves out semantic and sequence-to-sequence tasks like ASR, ST, or KS.
The explanation for the performance drop in the base-scale bidirectional setting remains somewhat speculative and lacks deeper mechanistic investigation.

strengths: Timely and well-motivated exploration: Systematic investigation of replacing Transformer backbones with Mamba in HuBERT pretraining, filling a gap in speech self-supervised representation learning.

Comprehensive empirical evaluation: The paper thoroughly covers runtime efficiency (MACs/sec and RTF up to 320s), fine-tuning under long-context and streaming/causal setups, internal representation diagnostics (phone purity, layer-wise CCA with phonemes, speakers, and emotion), and downstream probing tasks.

Convincing practical benefits in causal and long-context settings: Demonstrates clear efficiency advantages over Causal Transformers (avoiding OOM on full-document ASR, achieving lower WER with 17% fewer parameters in streaming ASR, and higher peak phone purity).

Balanced and transparent discussion: The authors openly present both strengths and weaknesses of Mamba SSL, explicitly documenting the performance drop of bidirectional Mamba at the base scale compared to standard bidirectional Transformers.
weaknesses: Sub-benchmark coverage: Probing evaluation relies only on a 4-task subset of SUPERB (PR, SID, ER, IC) rather than the full 10+ task suite, omitting tasks such as keyword spotting, slot filling, or speech separation.

Constrained pretraining budget: Due to single-GPU training constraints, the effective batch duration was roughly one-fourth of the canonical HuBERT setup, which may constrain overall model convergence despite fair side-by-side baselines.

Performance gap in standard bidirectional setting: At the Base model scale, ExtBiMamba and InnBiMamba still substantially underperform standard bidirectional Transformer on SUPERB (SUPERB score ~815-832 vs. 868.9), leaving bidirectional scaling largely unresolved.

Missing hyperparameter details: Specific Mamba architectural parameters (e.g., state expansion factor, convolution width, discretization step initialization) and fine-tuning learning rate schedules are not detailed in the main text.

strengths: Systematic and timely empirical exploration of applying Mamba state-space architectures to speech self-supervised learning (specifically within the HuBERT framework).
Comprehensive experimental setup covering computational efficiency (MACs, RTF vs. sequence duration up to 320 seconds), causal streaming ASR, long-context document-level ASR, and downstream probing.
Insightful representation analyses, including layer-wise phone purity under multiple cluster granularities and canonical correlation analysis (CCA) with phonetic, speaker, and emotion attributes.

Honest reporting and critical discussion of empirical limitations, particularly identifying that bidirectional Mamba models lag behind standard Transformers at base scale and discussing potential architectural reasons (e.g., ExtBiMamba vs. InnBiMamba).
weaknesses: The evaluation on SUPERB is limited to four selected tasks (PR, SID, ER, IC) rather than the complete 10-task benchmark, which somewhat restricts the breadth of downstream validation.

In the long-context ASR experiment, the Transformer baseline simply encounters out-of-memory (OOM) errors; the paper does not compare against common efficient attention adaptations (e.g., FlashAttention-2, block/sliding-window attention, or chunked processing).

Pre-training was conducted under computational constraints on a single GPU with reduced batch size (one-fourth of the original HuBERT audio volume per batch), meaning results are compared strictly against similarly trained baselines rather than fully scaled standard models.

strengths: The paper provides a timely, rigorous, and thorough investigation of Mamba within the HuBERT self-supervised learning framework, evaluating both causal (streaming) and bidirectional setups across fine-tuning, efficiency benchmarks, and representation probing.

The empirical findings are balanced and honest: the authors demonstrate clear advantages of Mamba in causal/streaming settings and long-context processing (e.g., document-level ASR on TED-LIUM 3 where Transformers encounter out-of-memory errors), while transparently reporting and analyzing its scalability gap compared to standard Transformers in base-scale bidirectional regimes.

The representational analyses (layer-wise phone purity, CCA with phonetic, speaker, and emotion embeddings, and loss-scale training stability diagnostics) provide valuable insights into how State Space Models organize acoustic and linguistic information differently from self-attention models.
weaknesses: Due to hardware constraints (single V100 GPU per model), the effective batch size is roughly one-fourth of the original HuBERT recipe. While this is controlled fairly against an in-house Transformer baseline, it results in absolute downstream performance that trails standard published benchmarks.

The long-context efficiency comparison evaluates vanilla self-attention against Mamba, omitting modernized Transformer baselines equipped with FlashAttention or linear/chunked attention variants (e.g., Emformer or Chunk Conformer), which are standard practical alternatives for streaming and long-context speech recognition.
All reported pretraining and fine-tuning results stem from single runs without error bars or variance reporting across random seeds.

strengths: Presents a timely, systematic, and comprehensive empirical exploration of integrating Mamba state space architectures into self-supervised speech representation learning (HuBERT).

Provides multi-faceted evaluations spanning computational efficiency benchmarks (MACs/sec and RTF up to 320 seconds), causal and long-context ASR fine-tuning, standardized probing on SUPERB, and layer-wise representational analyses (phone purity, CCA).

Demonstrates clear practical benefits for streaming/causal ASR and long-context speech recognition, showing that causal Mamba outperforms causal Transformers with fewer parameters and avoids the out-of-memory bottlenecks of full attention.

Transparently reports and investigates negative/mixed findings regarding bidirectional Mamba scaling, supported by architectural ablations (InnBiMamba vs. ExtBiMamba) and loss-scale training stability analyses.
weaknesses: Pre-training was conducted on a single GPU with an effective batch size approximately one-fourth that of canonical HuBERT setups, resulting in baselines that underperform official open-source checkpoints and leaving open the question of behavior under full-scale pre-training regimes.

For the long-context ASR comparison, standard Transformer full self-attention is the sole baseline; comparing against memory-efficient attention variants (e.g., FlashAttention, local/chunked attention, or sliding-window attention) would provide a more rigorous efficiency benchmark.

The exploration is limited strictly to the HuBERT masked unit prediction framework; it is not yet established whether findings generalize to contrastive (e.g., wav2vec 2.0) or purely autoregressive speech SSL objectives.
The codebase URL is omitted in the abstract/introduction, which slightly diminishes immediate reproducibility verification.

strengths: Comprehensive and multi-faceted empirical study: The paper systematically explores Mamba as a replacement for Transformer backbones in speech SSL (HuBERT), evaluating computational efficiency, long-context ASR fine-tuning, streaming/causal ASR, downstream probing on SUPERB, and internal representational characteristics (phone purity, CCA).

Strong evidence for causal speech SSL: The paper convincingly demonstrates that Mamba is naturally well-suited for causal settings, outperforming Causal Transformers on both causal ASR (15.77% vs. 16.66% WER with fewer parameters) and downstream causal SUPERB probing.

Convincing demonstration of linear-time scaling in long-context ASR: The document-level ASR evaluation on TED-LIUM 3 shows a clear practical advantage where Mamba processes entire documents without segmentation (achieving 11.08% WER), whereas the standard Transformer runs out of memory.

Insightful analysis of representation dynamics and training stability: The authors provide detailed representational analyses (phone purity, attribute-specific CCA) and conduct an honest, illuminating exploration of bidirectional Mamba architectures (ExtBiMamba vs. InnBiMamba), linking the scalability gap at base size to training loss-scale instability.
weaknesses: Constrained pretraining budget: Due to single-GPU hardware limitations, the pretraining was conducted with an effective batch duration approximately one-fourth that of the original HuBERT. While the authors fairly train their own Transformer baselines under the same budget, the resulting models underperform official pretrained checkpoints, leaving open whether these findings hold under standard large-batch multi-GPU scaling.

Absence of efficient Transformer baselines for long sequences: In Section 4.2, document-level ASR compares ExtBiMamba against a standard quadratic Transformer that encounters OOM. Comparing against common long-context audio methods (e.g., chunked/local attention, FlashAttention, or downsampled Conformer models) would provide a more rigorous efficiency benchmark.

Performance lag in base-scale bidirectional models: In the bidirectional setting at base scale, Mamba-based variants still lag substantially behind the Transformer baseline across multiple SUPERB tasks (PR, SID, IC), limiting Mamba's readiness as a general drop-in replacement for standard bidirectional speech SSL.
